Access and usage limits

Confirm before ordering: Product research, saved items and exports.

Ask SEOGBTools support to confirm what your plan includes and whether any usage caps apply.

Ecomhunt gives store owners a place to look for product ideas. Start with one audience and a clear problem. A shop for apartment renters, for example, might shortlist compact storage products that work without drilling. Record who would buy each item, what it replaces, and what you still need to verify.

Check the real cost

Ask the supplier for a quote to the country you plan to serve. Add shipping, payment fees, packaging, expected returns, and any other variable costs you cover. Compare the result with the price customers pay for similar products. A cheap unit can become expensive once a supplier charges extra for tracking or replacement orders.

Test one product at a time

Order a sample and record how long it takes to arrive. Photograph the actual item and write a listing that answers common questions about size and materials. Set a small test budget and decide what counts as useful evidence before spending it. Compare Ecomhunt's current plan features with the work you need to do and use SaleHoo as a related supplier research resource.

Compare discovery and sourcing separately

Use Ecomhunt to create a shortlist, then check whether you can actually buy and deliver each item. Imagine you shortlist three compact organizers for renters. One fits several cabinet sizes, one needs a specific door thickness, and one includes adhesive that could damage a painted surface. Ask for measurements and test each design before writing a listing. Use SaleHoo for the separate task of finding supplier candidates. Keep a dated record of what you verified with each supplier so that a promising product idea does not get confused with a confirmed offer.

Start with a customer problem you can describe

Product research is easier when you know who the store serves. Write down one problem in the words a customer would use. For an apartment organization shop, the problem might be that renters have little cupboard space and cannot drill into walls. That gives you a better starting point than a broad category like home accessories. A hanging shelf, a drawer divider, and a countertop rack can all solve parts of the same problem, but each brings different dimensions, shipping needs, and questions.

Set a few limits before browsing Ecomhunt. Choose a market, a target selling price, and a product size you can afford to ship. Write down features that would make a product unsuitable for your audience. A rack that needs screws can still be useful for another shop, but it may be a poor fit if your promise is storage without drilling. These limits help you reject weak ideas quickly.

Keep the first shortlist small. A spreadsheet with five candidates is easier to verify than a list of fifty screenshots. For each item, add the exact variation, the problem it solves, the likely customer, and one reason someone would choose it over a similar product. Leave a separate column for questions you cannot yet answer.

Read discovery data in context

A product discovery tool can surface items you might have missed and give you a starting point for comparing them. The value comes from what you do after finding an item. A listing can be old, based on another market, or refer to a different variation from the one you intend to sell. Record the source and date so you can tell whether a later quote refers to the same product.

If the tool shows advertising examples, use them to understand how sellers explain a product. Look at whether an ad shows the problem, demonstrates the product, or highlights a particular feature. An example can suggest questions worth answering. It cannot tell you the seller's actual margin, return rate, or cost per order. Do not build your budget around an assumption that a visible ad is profitable.

Use the same approach when you find engagement numbers or trend signals. Notice whether interest appears tied to a holiday, a viral video, or a specific country. A spike can be worth investigating, but it can fade before your sample arrives. For a product you plan to sell year-round, look for evidence of a recurring need and review whether the supplier can deliver reliably outside the season that first brought it attention.

Compare public offers like a shopper

Choose a few stores serving the market you plan to enter. Open the exact product pages and compare the details a shopper can verify. Record the listed dimensions, materials, colors, shipping promises, and return terms. When a store shows several options, check which variation the starting price applies to. A photo of the largest version next to the price of the smallest can make a comparison misleading.

Look at the complete offer. One seller might bundle two organizers and another might sell them separately. A lower sticker price could mean a higher delivered price after shipping. Take note of the differences without assuming that your customers will prefer the cheapest option. A clear size guide and reliable delivery may be more important to the audience you serve.

Read buyer reviews for repeated questions and complaints. For an over-door organizer, buyers may want to know if the door can close, how much space the hooks need, or whether the product scratches painted surfaces. Give those questions to the supplier and test them on the sample yourself where possible. Use what you learn to write a product description that sets a clear expectation.

Avoid copying the competitor's ad, photos, or product copy. Write down the type of evidence shoppers responded to or asked for, then create your own version from what you can verify. A close-up of the actual mounting hook and a ruler beside it can answer more than a polished photo that hides the part customers care about.

Ask suppliers for quotes you can compare

Send the same basic request to each supplier. Name the exact product, color, size, and shipping destination. Ask for the sample cost, delivery method, and a written price for the order sizes you are likely to place. Confirm what comes in the box and whether the supplier can provide the same variation consistently.

Ask how replacements work when a package arrives damaged or a part is missing. Find out who pays for return shipping and whether the supplier offers tracking. If you are dropshipping individual orders, ask what appears on the parcel and how quickly the supplier shares tracking details. These questions help you estimate the work your support team will have to do.

Compare responses using the actual product you intend to offer. A supplier may quote the standard size even though the listing photo shows a larger version. Ask for a current photo of the variation and request confirmation in writing. Keep the quote beside the sample record so it is easy to see if the product that arrived matches the price and specifications you were given.

Work out what a sale leaves you

The delivered cost includes more than the supplier's unit price. Add shipping and packaging you pay for, marketplace or payment fees, and an allowance for replacements or returns. Use amounts you can trace to quotes or your own store records. Give any estimate its own column so that a guessed cost does not look like a confirmed amount.

For example, suppose you plan to sell an organizer for $30. If the supplier charges $9 for the item, shipping costs $6, payment and platform fees total $2, and you set aside $2 for returns or support, $11 remains before advertising and other overhead. These are example figures. Replace them with numbers from your own quote and store. If a sale costs $8 to acquire, the remaining amount in this example drops to $3 before fixed costs.

Run another version with a worse outcome. Check what happens if shipping costs more, if a discount reduces the selling price, or if several orders need replacements. A product with a narrow margin may become hard to support once the real costs arrive. If the numbers only work when every assumption is favorable, move the item down the shortlist or look for a different offer.

Test the sample and write the page from it

Order a sample before you advertise a product you have never handled. Record the actual delivery time from order to arrival and compare it with the supplier's quote. Open the parcel as a customer would. Check whether the instructions make sense, whether all parts are included, and whether the packaging is likely to protect the item during normal shipping.

Try the product in the setting you plan to show. For an apartment organizer, test the hook on the relevant door sizes, check how the door closes, and photograph the fitting from a few angles. If the product only works within a certain measurement range, put that range close to the buy button and show customers how to measure. A useful description can prevent a purchase that would otherwise turn into a return.

Write the listing around the results you can show. Include the size, material, included parts, fitting steps, and any limits buyers need to know. Use a photo of the real variation. State the delivery estimate and returns process where shoppers can find them before ordering. If the sample fails an important check, pause the test until you can verify a better version.

Run a small test with a clear decision

Pick one product, one audience, and one reason to buy. For example, test an organizer with renters who need extra storage without drilling. Make one creative that shows how it fits and another that shows what it can hold. Keep the offer and page consistent so you can see whether the different messages attract people who understand the product.

Decide what you will review before the campaign starts. Record how many visitors reach the page, add the item to their cart, and finish an order. Check what buyers ask after the sale. If many people ask whether the product fits, the listing may need clearer measurements. If they add the item to their cart and stop after seeing shipping charges, the total cost deserves a closer look.

Set a maximum spend and a date to review the test. If it ends with too few sales to draw a strong conclusion, record that result plainly. If you receive orders, compare the real costs and support work with your forecast. The next action might be to improve the page, negotiate a different shipping option, or stop selling the product. A short written review helps you remember what the test actually proved.

Compare Ecomhunt access with other research options

Check the current feature list and billing terms for the plan you are considering. Write down what your workflow needs, such as access to product ideas, filters for your target market, or the ability to keep a shortlist. Confirm which of those features are available in the offer at checkout. Plan names, trial terms, and limits can change.

Use the same task to compare tools. For a product discovery tool, measure how quickly you can shortlist relevant ideas and verify the data behind them. For a supplier directory, measure how many usable quotes you can get for the exact variation and destination. For an ad research tool, check whether the examples show enough detail to help you write and test your own message. The results of one task do not replace the other two.

Before buying, take one current product idea through your usual workflow and count the steps that consume the most time. A store that struggles to find relevant ideas may value discovery tools. A store that already has enough ideas but waits weeks for supplier replies may benefit more from improving sourcing. Review Ecomhunt for current product information and Pexda for another product research workflow.

Frequently asked questions

Does Ecomhunt tell me what to sell? It can help you discover ideas to research. Check each product against your audience, supplier options, and delivered cost before you decide whether to sell it.

How many products should I shortlist? Start with a number you can verify within the time available. For a small shop, a few items with comparable quotes and sample plans can be more useful than a large list you never review.

Can I estimate profit from the supplier price? You need the full selling and fulfillment costs. Include shipping, payment fees, returns, and advertising where applicable. Track the actual costs after launch so you can compare them with your estimate.

Do I need a sample for every candidate? Start by removing items that fail obvious checks, such as a poor fit for your audience or a delivered cost that leaves too little room. Order a sample for the item you plan to advertise and make sure it matches the exact variation you will list.

What should I do after the first test? Review which customers arrived, what they asked, what the orders cost to fulfill, and whether the sample matched what was delivered. Use that record to pick one change or decide that the product is a poor fit.

Review price, shipping and local competition when evaluating a product’s apparent popularity.
